processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Melted in a high-frequency vacuum induction furnace with a 50 kg capacity and cast into an ingot with a diameter of 150 mm.
Ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h before hot rolling.
Homogenized ingots were hot rolled into rods with a diameter of 16 mm, then air-cooled to room temperature (parent process proc_hot-rolled).

processing_steps.method: solution treatment followed by water quenching
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Hot-rolled rods were solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching (state label 1050 °C–2 h–WQ).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: EBSD system attached to a field emission gun SEM (FEI Quanta 650, Thermo Fisher Scientific)
characterization_methods.key_findings: For 1.0%C only austenite is present (no ferrite); coarse austenite grains with abundant twin boundaries; D_FCC-G/T = 23.7 ± 1.3 μm and f_Tw = 53.9% for C-1.0.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Operating voltage 20 kV, step size 0.5 μm; specimens mechanically ground and electro-polished in 7% Nital at room temperature; average grain size by linear intercept method with 15° boundary misorientation using Channel 5 software
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine phase distribution (FCC austenite / BCC ferrite) and grain size as a function of C, Mn and Al content

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: TEM (Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN, Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at 200 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: Nano-sized κ-carbides uniformly distributed in the austenite; average κ-carbide diameter 3.0 ± 0.6 nm for C-1.0 (Table 3); orientation relationship (001)κ || (001)γ; SAED κ spots weak due to short-range ordering.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Thin foils prepared by twin-jet electro-polishing in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 20 V and −20 °C; dark-field imaging along [001]γ using a κ-carbide reflection
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize κ-carbide size, distribution and orientation relationship with the austenite matrix
characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) dark-field imaging with SAED

analytical_models.equation_role: Predict alloy density (g/cm³) as a function of C, Al and Mn content (mass%)
analytical_models.model_note: ρ = 8.10 − 0.102C − 0.10Al − 0.01Mn (Eq. 3); applied to this composition gives 6.6 g/cm³.

computational_details.simulation_method: linear least-squares fitting of experimental density data (analytical model)
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Eq. (3) gives 6.6 g/cm³ for Fe30Mn11Al1.0C, matching the experimental value 6.60 g/cm³ (Table 1), whereas the earlier Ref. [4] coefficients give 6.29 g/cm³.

analytical_models.equation_role: Shear strength contribution from coherent κ-carbides
analytical_models.model_note: σ_shear = α f^(1/2) d_Car^(1/2) (Eq. 4); derived slope of yield strength vs d_Car^0.5 = 97.1 MPa/nm^1/2 (R_p0.2 = 478 + 97.1 d_Car^0.5), flow stress without κ-carbide strengthening ≈ 478 MPa.

computational_details.simulation_method: analytical particle-shear strengthening model with linear least-squares fitting of yield strength vs d_Car^0.5
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Linear fit of yield strength against the square root of κ-carbide size over the solution-treated steels gives slope 97.1 MPa/nm^1/2 and intercept 478 MPa; particle shear strengthening remains active up to κ-carbide sizes ~50 nm.

interfaces.interface_notes: The κ-carbides are coherent with the austenite matrix; particle shear strengthening was found still active up to κ-carbide sizes as large as 50 nm, well above the typical ~5 nm shearing-to-Orowan transition size.
interfaces.phase_evolution: κ-carbides precipitate from spinodal decomposition and ordering of C and Al in austenite and coarsen with increasing C and Al content; no ferrite remains at the reference 1.0C/11Al/30Mn composition.
interfaces.slip_behavior: The κ-carbide strengthening contribution is described by a particle shear model (Eq. 4) rather than an Orowan mechanism; shear deformation facilitates glide of dislocations across κ-carbide shear planes, weakening work hardening.

defects.type: twin boundaries (Σ3); fractional twin boundary length f_Tw = 53.9%

phases_present.morphology: equiaxed grains with abundant twin boundaries; only austenite is present

precipitates.coherency: coherent interface with the austenite matrix
precipitates.distribution: uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix

microstructure_list.region: bulk rod (no local region distinction reported)

structures.overall_structure: After solution treatment at 1050 °C for 2 h + water quenching the C-1.0 (Fe30Mn11Al1.0C) steel consists of a single austenite (γ, FCC) phase with no ferrite, containing uniformly distributed nano-sized κ-carbides; austenite grains are coarse and rich in annealing twin boundaries (Σ3).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: MTS tensile machine; data are the average of two solution-treated specimens; stress-strain jumps after yielding caused by extensometer removal
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: round tensile specimen, gauge length 25 mm and diameter 5 mm, tensile axis parallel to the rod axis

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: MTS impact tester (500 J capacity); data are the average of two specimens; value is Charpy V-notch impact energy Akv (−40 °C), not a fracture-toughness K value
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: Charpy specimen 55 mm long, 10 × 10 mm cross-section, 2 mm deep V-notch perpendicular to the rod axis

unmapped_findings: For C-1.0 (Fe30Mn11Al1.0C) after 1050 °C/2 h solution treatment, the maximum true stress just before necking (σ_TS, crack nucleation) = 1343 MPa and the fracture strength (σ_FS) = 2095 MPa (Table 2, footnote a).
Fractional twin boundary length f_Tw = 53.9% for the C-1.0 sample as measured by EBSD (Table 3); no ferrite fraction (f_Bcc) or ferrite grain size (D_Bcc) are reported for C-1.0 (dashes in Table 3).
Density of the Fe30Mn11Al1.0C composition predicted by Eq. (3) is 6.6 g/cm³, matching the experimental Archimedes value of 6.60 g/cm³ (the earlier Ref. [4] coefficients would give 6.29 g/cm³).

Slight inconsistency in κ-carbide size for 1.0%C across the paper: the text (b0044) states the average κ-carbide diameter is about 2.0 nm for the 1.0%C steel, whereas Table 3 lists 3.0 ± 0.6 nm (and the 30%Mn/11%Al rows of Table 3 also list 3.0 ± 0.6 nm).

The engineering stress-strain curve for the 1.0%C steel after 1050 °C solution treatment (Fig. 2(a) / Fig. 1 second panel) shows it to be weaker but far more ductile than the higher-C steels, failing beyond ~55-63% strain (red curve).

The C-1.0 composition corresponds to three identical entries in the tables (C-1.0, Mn-30, Al-11 = Fe-1.00C-30.07Mn-11.07Al); its chemistry is C 1.00, Mn 30.07, Al 11.07, Fe Bal (mass%) with density 6.60 g/cm³.

Except for the 0.6C and 30Mn steels the work-hardening rate vs true strain shows a typical rapid drop, slow rise then second drop; the 30Mn (i.e. this C-1.0) steel instead shows a monotonic decrease of work hardening rate with increasing true strain (Fig. 8).
